demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: go over and over why the event happened to me
try hard not think about the trauma
Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost

Threat.value: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory

issues.item: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction
issues.explanation: Several selected items imply a hypervigilance/physical-assault style threat profile (scanning exits, reacting to sudden movements, avoiding open spaces) that is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one. These items usually fit interpersonal violence, combat, or other danger-based trauma more than bereavement trauma.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: 'Rehearse Conversations before any interaction' suggests prominent social-evaluative anxiety, but there are no corresponding threat or memory items about social humiliation, blame, or feared conversations about the death. It sits awkwardly with the rest of the profile and does not clearly connect to the active Memory→Threat→Strategies formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
issues.explanation: These items imply a danger-based, assault-like or combat-like threat profile centered on physical attack and environmental vulnerability, which is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of unexpected death of a loved one.

issues.item: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The threat content is internally coherent with hypervigilance for interpersonal/physical danger, but that pattern is not clinically well matched to the rest of the profile, where memory items reflect disorganized recall of a death-related trauma rather than threat from current spaces, exits, or others' movements.

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: 'Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard' is more typical of interpersonal violence/combat threat cues and is hard to reconcile with a trauma of unexpected death of a loved one when the rest of the profile centers on grief-related memory disturbance rather than current danger from people.

vignette:
Kwame Mensah was 62 when he came for treatment, a divorced African American stock broker who had spent decades in fast-moving trading rooms where composure, quick judgment, and appetite for risk were treated almost as professional virtues. He spoke about his former wife only in passing, but when he described the death of the woman he lost, his voice changed. She had been his long-term partner, the person he called at market close, the one who knew the rhythm of his days. Her death had been sudden and traumatic, the kind of phone call that divides life into before and after. He still remembered seeing her name on his screen and then, later, the jarring fragments that followed: being told there had been an emergency, the rush to get there, the sight of her body, the unbearable fact that only minutes earlier he had assumed there would be another ordinary evening together.

What stayed with him was not a clean, tellable story. He said the memory came "in shards." At odd moments, a piece would strike him with no warning-the look of the room, the sound of someone speaking too calmly, the angle of her hand-and then vanish before he could make sense of it. When he tried on purpose to remember what happened from beginning to end, he found himself blank, as though the middle had been cut out. He knew there were details he must have lived through, but he could not reach them deliberately. That missingness troubled him as much as the images themselves. He had come to believe there was something wrong with him for not being able to hold the whole picture, and so he would spend late nights going over and over why this had happened to him, why he had this life and then had it torn open, why he was left with only scraps.

In the months after her death, he began trying hard not to think about it at all. He removed photographs from visible places in his apartment, stopped taking the route that passed the restaurant where they used to meet after work, and turned away whenever friends tried to mention her. Anything that reminded him of someone he had lost felt intolerable. He told himself that if he allowed one memory in, the rest would follow and he would not be able to contain it. At work he became especially rigid about this rule. The trading floor, with its constant alerts, ringing phones, and abrupt surges of urgency, was already intense; he now used the pace of it to crowd out anything personal. Still, reminders broke through. A female client with his partner's perfume, a colleague casually asking about weekend plans, a news segment on a sudden death playing on a monitor in the office lounge-these moments could stop him cold. For a few seconds he would feel as if he were back in that original scene, not remembering it but inside it. Once, after hearing a phone ring in a pattern like the call he had received that day, he stood frozen at his desk, heart pounding, staring past his monitors while a junior analyst had to repeat his name twice.

He described living with strong waves of fear, anger, guilt, and shame, often without warning. At times he was furious at the randomness of what had happened; at others he felt guilty for still being alive, guilty for details he could not even fully retrieve, guilty that he had not somehow prevented the loss. He was ashamed of how shaken he could become in situations other people seemed to move through easily. To counter that feeling, he started taking risks in ways that worried him even as he did them. He drove aggressively after late shifts, made impulsive decisions with money outside his usual disciplined strategy, and at times seemed almost daring harm to come close. He did not describe this as wanting to die. It was more that caution no longer felt meaningful in the same way, and moments of danger briefly cut through the deadened unreality that had settled over much of his life.

Over time these habits narrowed his world. Friends stopped inviting him out because he so often refused if the outing might stir memories. At the office, where he had once been known as exacting but steady, colleagues began noticing abrupt absences, uncharacteristic recklessness, and the way he sometimes went silent after an unexpected cue. He sought help only after a recent episode in which a fragment of the memory came over him during a volatile trading morning; for several moments he felt he was there again, and afterward he was so rattled that he left the floor early. Sitting in treatment, Kwame said he was tired of living as if his life were organized around dodging reminders and bracing for the next ambush from his own mind. What frightened him most was that the memory would either swallow him whole or remain forever broken and unreachable. What he hoped, cautiously, was not to forget her, but to be able to carry what happened without feeling that any ordinary day could suddenly become that day again.
